topic: The Christmas Bird Count: Counting Instead of Shooting
zh: 聖誕數鳥活動：用數鳥取代打鳥
src: National Audubon Society · Rosenberg et al., Science (2019)

a.title: Counting Birds for Christmas
text: Every year from December 14 to January 5, thousands of people go outside with notebooks and binoculars. They are not shopping for gifts. They are counting birds. This event is called the Christmas Bird Count, and it is one of the oldest citizen science projects in the world.

It started in 1900. Back then, some Americans had a strange holiday game called the "side hunt." Teams went out and shot as many birds as they could, and the team with the most dead birds won. A bird expert named Frank Chapman did not like this game. He had a better idea: count the birds instead of killing them. On Christmas Day that year, 27 people joined his first count.

Today, the rules are simple. Each group counts birds in a circle about 24 kilometers wide, and they do it on one day. They write down every bird they see or hear. Beginners can join an experienced birder, so you don't need to be an expert.

Why is this important? Scientists use the numbers to learn which birds are doing well and which are in danger. The data have shown that many kinds of birds are moving to new places as the weather changes.

Taiwan has a similar event. Every New Year, bird lovers around the island go out and count birds together. So this winter, look up! The bird outside your window might be part of an important science project.
tz: 每年 12 月 14 日到 1 月 5 日，成千上萬的人帶著筆記本和雙筒望遠鏡到戶外。他們不是去買禮物，而是去數鳥。這個活動叫做「聖誕數鳥」，是世界上歷史最悠久的公民科學計畫之一。
它從 1900 年開始。當時有些美國人有一種奇怪的節日遊戲，叫做「邊打獵」。各隊出去盡可能多射殺鳥，打死最多鳥的隊伍獲勝。一位名叫法蘭克・查普曼的鳥類專家不喜歡這個遊戲。他有個更好的主意：把鳥數一數，而不是殺掉牠們。那年的聖誕節，有 27 個人參加了他的第一次數鳥活動。
現在的規則很簡單。每一組在直徑大約 24 公里的圓形範圍內數鳥，而且只在一天之內完成。他們把看到或聽到的每一隻鳥都記下來。新手可以跟著有經驗的賞鳥人一起，所以你不必是專家。
為什麼這件事很重要？科學家用這些數字來了解哪些鳥過得好、哪些鳥面臨危險。這些資料顯示，隨著天氣的變化，很多種鳥正搬到新的地方。
台灣也有類似的活動。每逢新年，全島的愛鳥人士會一起出門數鳥。所以這個冬天，抬頭看看吧！你窗外的那隻鳥，也許就是一項重要科學計畫的一部分。

b.title: The Christmas Bird Count: A Century of Citizen Science
text: For most people, the weeks before Christmas mean shopping lists and holiday parties. For tens of thousands of volunteers across the Americas and beyond, they mean something else: a day spent outdoors, counting every bird in sight. The Christmas Bird Count, which runs from December 14 to January 5 each year, is one of the longest-running wildlife surveys on Earth.

The project began as a protest. In the late 1800s, a popular holiday tradition in North America was the "side hunt," in which teams competed to shoot the most birds and other animals. At the same time, many bird populations were falling sharply, partly because feathers were in demand for women's hats. In 1900, Frank Chapman, an ornithologist and the editor of a bird magazine, proposed a gentler competition: counting birds rather than killing them. Twenty-seven people took part in the first count.

The method has hardly changed since then. Each count takes place within a fixed circle about 24 kilometers across, and volunteers record every bird they see or hear on a single day. Because the same circles are surveyed year after year, the results can be compared over decades, and that is what makes them valuable.

Scientists have relied on these records to track long-term trends. Together with other surveys, they contributed to a major 2019 study which estimated that North America had lost nearly three billion birds since 1970. The data have also shown many species shifting their winter ranges northward, a pattern linked to a warming climate.

The count has limits, of course. Volunteers vary in skill, some areas are covered far better than others, and bad weather can lower the numbers on count day. Researchers use statistical methods to adjust for these differences, but the data are best at showing broad trends rather than exact totals.

Similar projects now exist around the world, including Taiwan's New Year bird count. Their message is the same: you do not need a laboratory to do real science. A pair of binoculars, a notebook and some patience may be enough.
tz: 對大多數人來說，聖誕節前的幾週意味著購物清單和節日派對。但對美洲及其他地區數以萬計的志工而言，這段時間代表另一件事：花一天待在戶外，把眼前看到的每一隻鳥都數下來。每年 12 月 14 日到 1 月 5 日舉行的聖誕數鳥，是地球上持續最久的野生動物調查之一。
這個計畫起初是一種抗議。1800 年代後期，北美流行一種節日傳統叫「邊打獵」，各隊比賽誰射殺最多鳥類和其他動物。同一時間，許多鳥類族群數量正急劇下降，部分原因是女性帽子上的羽毛需求很大。1900 年，鳥類學家、也是一本鳥類雜誌編輯的法蘭克・查普曼，提議一種比較溫和的比賽：數鳥，而不是殺鳥。第一次數鳥有二十七人參加。
從那時起，方法幾乎沒有改變。每一次數鳥都在一個直徑約 24 公里的固定圓形範圍內進行，志工在一天之內記錄看到或聽到的每一隻鳥。因為同樣的圓圈年復一年地被調查，結果可以跨越數十年互相比較，而這正是它們珍貴的地方。
科學家依靠這些紀錄來追蹤長期趨勢。這些資料和其他調查一起，促成了 2019 年一項重要研究，估計北美自 1970 年以來減少了將近三十億隻鳥。資料也顯示許多物種的越冬範圍正往北移，這種模式和氣候暖化有關。
當然，數鳥活動也有它的限制。志工的程度不一，有些地區比其他地區調查得仔細得多，而壞天氣也可能讓數鳥當天的數字偏低。研究人員會用統計方法來校正這些差異，但這些資料最擅長呈現大致的趨勢，而不是精確的總數。
現在世界各地都有類似的計畫，包括台灣的新年數鳥活動。它們傳達的訊息都一樣：做真正的科學不一定需要實驗室。一副雙筒望遠鏡、一本筆記本，再加上一點耐心，或許就夠了。

c.title: The Power and Limits of Citizen Science
text: On a cold morning in mid-December, a retired teacher, a high-school student and a dentist may find themselves standing in the same muddy field, binoculars raised, arguing over whether a small brown bird is a sparrow or a finch. Such scenes are repeated thousands of times during the Christmas Bird Count, an annual survey that has run since 1900. It is a reminder that some of the most valuable data in ecology are gathered not by professionals but by amateurs.

The count's origins are unusually well documented. It was proposed by the ornithologist Frank Chapman as a peaceful alternative to the "side hunt," a holiday contest in which teams tried to shoot as many birds as possible. Chapman's idea was modest, yet it anticipated a principle that modern ecology depends on: long, consistent records matter more than any single dramatic observation.

That principle explains the count's scientific value. Because volunteers return to the same circles each winter, researchers can detect slow changes that no short study could reveal. Such records helped scientists document the northward drift of many wintering species, and they contributed to a widely reported 2019 estimate that North America had lost nearly three billion birds since 1970.

Yet the very features that make citizen science powerful also make it vulnerable. Observers differ enormously in skill; an expert may identify forty species where a beginner sees twenty. Effort is uneven, too: circles near cities and wealthy areas tend to be surveyed more thoroughly than remote ones, which can distort the picture. Sceptics also note that a rise in sightings may reflect more birdwatchers rather than more birds.

Researchers have not ignored these problems. Modern analyses adjust for the number of observers and the hours they spend in the field, and projects such as eBird ask users to record how long and how far they searched. These corrections cannot remove every bias, but they turn a hobby into a dataset that can be tested and improved.

There is also a debate about the word "citizen" itself. Some organizations now prefer the term "community science," arguing that taking part should not depend on nationality. The change may seem cosmetic, but it reflects a broader goal: to make science feel open to anyone who is curious.

Perhaps the deepest value of the count is not in its numbers at all. A person who has spent a frozen morning counting birds is more likely to notice when they begin to disappear. In that sense, the survey produces not only data but also witnesses.
tz: 十二月中旬一個寒冷的早晨，一位退休老師、一名高中生和一位牙醫，可能會發現自己站在同一片泥濘的田野上，舉著雙筒望遠鏡，爭論一隻棕色小鳥到底是麻雀還是雀科的其他鳥。在聖誕數鳥期間，這樣的場景會重複上演成千上萬次；這項年度調查從 1900 年持續至今。它提醒我們，生態學裡一些最珍貴的資料，不是由專業人士、而是由業餘者蒐集的。
這項活動的起源有非常完整的紀錄。它由鳥類學家法蘭克・查普曼提出，作為「邊打獵」的和平替代方案；「邊打獵」是一種節日競賽，各隊設法射殺越多鳥越好。查普曼的構想並不宏大，卻預示了現代生態學所依賴的一項原則：長期、一致的紀錄，比任何一次戲劇性的觀察都更重要。
這項原則說明了數鳥的科學價值。因為志工每年冬天都回到同樣的圓圈，研究人員才能偵測出任何短期研究都無法揭示的緩慢變化。這類紀錄幫助科學家記錄到許多越冬物種向北移動，也促成了 2019 年一項廣受報導的估計：北美自 1970 年以來減少了將近三十億隻鳥。
然而，讓公民科學強大的那些特點，也正是它容易出問題的地方。觀察者的程度差異極大；專家可能辨識出四十種鳥，新手卻只看到二十種。投入的心力也不平均：靠近城市和富裕地區的圓圈，往往比偏遠地區調查得更徹底，這可能扭曲整體樣貌。懷疑者也指出，目擊紀錄增加，可能反映的是賞鳥人變多，而不是鳥變多。
研究人員並沒有忽視這些問題。現代的分析會根據觀察者人數和他們在野外花的時數做校正，而像 eBird 這樣的計畫也要求使用者記錄自己找了多久、走了多遠。這些校正無法消除所有偏差，但它們把一項嗜好變成可以被檢驗、被改進的資料集。
關於「公民」這個詞本身也有爭論。現在有些組織比較喜歡用「社群科學」這個說法，認為參與與否不該取決於國籍。這個改變看似只是表面功夫，卻反映了一個更廣的目標：讓任何有好奇心的人都覺得科學向他們敞開。
也許數鳥最深層的價值根本不在數字上。一個曾在凍人的早晨數過鳥的人，更有可能在鳥開始消失時察覺到。從這個意義上說，這項調查產出的不只是資料，還有見證者。

b.title: One Plant, Many Teas
text: If you walk into a tea shop in Taiwan, the menu can be overwhelming: green tea, black tea, oolong, jasmine, Oriental Beauty and dozens of milk teas. It may surprise you to learn that almost all of them come from a single plant, Camellia sinensis. What turns the same green leaf into so many different drinks is not the plant itself but what happens after the leaves are picked.

The key process is called oxidation. When tea leaves are cut, rolled or crushed, their cells break and the leaves react with oxygen in the air, slowly turning darker, much like a sliced apple turning brown. Tea makers control this reaction carefully. To make green tea, they heat the leaves soon after picking, which stops oxidation almost completely. To make black tea, they let the leaves oxidize fully before drying them.

Oolong tea sits between these two extremes, and it is the type for which Taiwan is best known. Its leaves are only partly oxidized, so oolongs can taste anything from fresh and flowery to deep and roasted. High-mountain oolongs grown in places such as Alishan are prized for their smooth taste, which comes partly from the cool, misty climate.

One Taiwanese tea has an unusual helper. Oriental Beauty is made from leaves that have been bitten by tiny insects called tea green leafhoppers. The plant reacts to the bites by producing natural chemicals, which give the tea a sweet, honey-like flavor. For this reason, farmers who grow it must avoid using pesticides.

Taiwan's most famous modern invention, bubble tea, took tea in a completely new direction. Created in the 1980s, it combined sweetened tea, milk and chewy tapioca balls, and it has since spread to cities around the world. Some critics point out, however, that a large cup can contain more sugar than doctors recommend for an entire day.

International Tea Day, celebrated on December 15 by many tea-growing countries, is a good reason to slow down and taste the difference. Whichever cup you choose, you are drinking the result of careful decisions made by farmers and tea makers.
tz: 走進台灣的手搖飲店，菜單可能多到讓人眼花撩亂：綠茶、紅茶、烏龍、茉莉、東方美人，還有幾十種奶茶。你可能會很驚訝，它們幾乎都來自同一種植物——茶樹（Camellia sinensis）。讓同一片綠葉變成這麼多種飲料的，不是植物本身，而是茶葉採下之後發生的事。
關鍵的過程叫做氧化。茶葉被切、揉或壓碎時，細胞會破裂，葉子和空氣中的氧氣起反應，慢慢變深色，就像切開的蘋果會變褐色一樣。製茶師會小心控制這個反應。做綠茶時，他們在採摘後不久就加熱茶葉，幾乎完全停止氧化；做紅茶時，則讓茶葉完全氧化之後再乾燥。
烏龍茶介於這兩個極端之間，也是台灣最有名的茶類。它的葉子只部分氧化，所以烏龍的味道可以從清新花香一路到濃郁焙火。像阿里山這些地方種的高山烏龍，以滑順的口感受到珍視，這部分來自涼爽多霧的氣候。
有一種台灣茶有個不尋常的幫手。東方美人茶是用被一種叫小綠葉蟬的小昆蟲咬過的葉子做成的。茶樹會對這些咬傷做出反應，產生天然的化學物質，讓茶帶有甜甜的蜂蜜香。因為這個原因，種植它的農夫必須避免使用農藥。
台灣最有名的現代發明——珍珠奶茶，把茶帶往完全不同的方向。它在 1980 年代誕生，結合了加糖的茶、牛奶和有嚼勁的粉圓，之後傳到了世界各地的城市。不過也有批評者指出，一大杯珍奶含的糖可能比醫生建議一整天攝取的量還多。
許多產茶國家在 12 月 15 日慶祝國際茶日，這是個放慢腳步、品嘗其中差異的好理由。無論你選哪一杯，你喝下的都是農夫和製茶師細心抉擇的成果。

c.title: The Bitter History of a Gentle Drink
text: Few drinks seem as peaceful as tea. It is associated with quiet afternoons, polite conversation and moments of calm. Yet the history of the tea trade is anything but gentle. Over the past three centuries, the demand for this humble leaf has helped spark protests, finance wars and reshape the lives of millions of workers.

Consider the most famous tea party in history. On December 16, 1773, colonists in Boston boarded British ships and dumped hundreds of chests of tea into the harbor. Their anger was not really about the drink; it was about being taxed by a parliament in which they had no representatives. The protest became one of the sparks of the American Revolution.

Across the world, Britain's growing thirst for Chinese tea created a different crisis. Because China wanted little that Britain produced, British merchants paid for tea largely in silver. To reverse this flow, traders began selling opium grown in British India to China, despite Chinese bans. When Chinese officials destroyed large stocks of the drug, the result was the First Opium War of 1839 to 1842, which forced China to open its ports and hand over Hong Kong.

Britain then set out to end its dependence on China altogether. In the late 1840s, the botanist Robert Fortune travelled through China in disguise and smuggled thousands of tea plants and seeds to India. Combined with a native tea variety found in Assam, these efforts helped build vast plantations, which often relied on poorly paid workers living in harsh conditions.

Those conditions have not entirely disappeared. Tea is the world's most widely consumed drink after water, yet many of the people who pick it still earn wages that are hard to live on. It is no accident that International Tea Day, first held on December 15, 2005, was promoted by trade unions and campaigners in tea-producing countries; its purpose was to draw attention to workers' rights and fair prices.

Some argue that this history is too distant to matter to a modern student ordering a drink. But the questions it raises are strikingly current. Who grows what we consume? Who benefits from its price? Labels such as fair trade are imperfect answers, but they show that consumers can at least ask.

None of this means we should stop enjoying tea. It means that a cup of tea, like many ordinary objects, carries a long chain of human decisions inside it. Tasting it fully may include knowing where it came from.
tz: 很少有飲料看起來像茶這麼平和。它讓人聯想到安靜的午後、有禮的交談和片刻的寧靜。然而，茶葉貿易的歷史一點也不溫和。過去三個世紀以來，對這片不起眼葉子的需求，曾助長抗爭、資助戰爭，並改變了數百萬工人的人生。
想想歷史上最有名的茶會。1773 年 12 月 16 日，波士頓的殖民地居民登上英國船隻，把數百箱茶葉倒進港口。他們的憤怒其實不在於茶本身，而是在於被一個他們沒有代表的國會課稅。這場抗議成為美國獨立革命的導火線之一。
在世界的另一端，英國對中國茶日益增長的渴求造成了另一場危機。因為中國幾乎不需要英國生產的東西，英國商人買茶主要用白銀支付。為了扭轉這股白銀外流，商人開始把英屬印度種植的鴉片賣到中國，無視中國的禁令。當中國官員銷毀大批鴉片後，結果就是 1839 到 1842 年的第一次鴉片戰爭，迫使中國開放港口並割讓香港。
接著，英國著手徹底擺脫對中國的依賴。1840 年代後期，植物學家羅伯特・福鈞喬裝走遍中國，把數千株茶苗和茶種走私到印度。這些行動加上在阿薩姆發現的本土茶種，幫助建立起廣大的茶園，而這些茶園往往仰賴薪資微薄、生活條件惡劣的工人。
這樣的處境並沒有完全消失。茶是全世界除了水以外最多人喝的飲料，但許多採茶的人賺的工資仍然難以維生。2005 年 12 月 15 日首次舉辦的國際茶日，由產茶國的工會和倡議人士推動，這並非偶然；它的目的是讓人們關注工人的權利和公平的價格。
有些人認為，這段歷史太遙遠了，和一個點飲料的現代學生沒什麼關係。但它提出的問題其實非常切身。誰種出了我們消費的東西？誰從它的價格中獲益？像「公平貿易」這樣的標章雖然不是完美的答案，但至少顯示消費者可以發問。
這一切並不代表我們應該停止享受茶。而是意味著，一杯茶就像許多日常物品一樣，裡面承載著一長串人類的抉擇。要完整地品嘗它，或許也包括知道它從哪裡來。

a.title: Why We Think We Know More Than We Do
text: Have you ever finished a test and felt sure you got everything right, but then you got a low score? You are not alone. Psychologists call this kind of mistake the Dunning-Kruger effect. It means that people who know very little about something often think they know a lot.

The idea comes from two American psychologists, David Dunning and Justin Kruger. In 1999, they gave college students tests on grammar, logic and humor. Then they asked the students to guess how well they did. The students with the lowest scores thought they did much better than most other people. In fact, they did worse than most of their classmates.

Why does this happen? Dunning and Kruger had a simple answer. To know that you are wrong, you need the same skills that you need to be right. If you don't know much grammar, you can't see your own grammar mistakes. So you feel confident, even when you are not doing well.
Interestingly, the students with the best scores thought they did a little worse than they really did. Because the test felt easy to them, they thought it was easy for everyone.

What can we learn? Everyone is a beginner at something. Before you say "I'm sure," ask a teacher or a friend to check your work. Learning more may make you feel less sure at first, but that is a good sign.
tz: 你有沒有考完試覺得自己全部答對，結果分數卻很低？你不是唯一這樣的人。心理學家把這種錯誤叫做「達克效應」。它的意思是：對某件事懂得很少的人，常常以為自己懂很多。
這個概念來自兩位美國心理學家：大衛・達寧和賈斯汀・克魯格。1999 年，他們讓大學生做文法、邏輯和幽默感的測驗，接著請學生猜自己考得怎麼樣。分數最低的學生以為自己比大多數人考得好很多；事實上，他們考得比大多數同學都差。
為什麼會這樣？達寧和克魯格給了一個簡單的答案：要知道自己錯了，需要的能力和要做對時需要的能力是一樣的。如果你文法懂得不多，你就看不出自己的文法錯誤。所以即使表現不好，你還是覺得很有自信。
有趣的是，分數最好的學生反而以為自己考得比實際上差一點。因為他們覺得考試很簡單，就以為對每個人來說都很簡單。
我們可以學到什麼？每個人在某件事上都是初學者。在你說「我很確定」之前，請老師或朋友幫你檢查一下。多學一點，一開始可能會讓你覺得比較沒把握，但那是個好跡象。

ph.ex: At first I was nervous, but then I had fun.
ph.exzh: 一開始我很緊張，但後來玩得很開心。

q.q: What is the reading mainly about?
opts: Why people with less skill may feel too confident
How to get a higher score on a grammar test
Why college tests are too hard for most students
How two psychologists became good friends
q.why: 第 1 段定義達克效應，第 2–4 段說明實驗與原因，第 5 段給建議——重點是能力不足的人容易過度自信。

q.q: According to the reading, which is TRUE?
opts: The students with the lowest scores knew they did badly.
Dunning and Kruger did their study in 1999.
The best students thought they did much better than they did.
The tests in the study were about math and science.
q.why: 第 2 段：In 1999, they gave college students tests…。第 2 段低分者以為自己考很好；第 4 段高分者低估自己；第 2 段測驗是文法、邏輯、幽默。

q.q: In paragraph 4, what does “it” in “it was easy for everyone” refer to?
opts: the score
the student
the grammar
the test
q.why: 第 4 段：Because the test felt easy to them, they thought it was easy for everyone——it 指測驗。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “confident” means ___.
opts: feeling tired and sleepy
feeling angry with others
feeling sure about yourself
feeling afraid of mistakes
q.why: 第 3 段：So you feel confident, even when you are not doing well——覺得有把握、有自信。

q.q: What can we learn from paragraph 3?
opts: People who study grammar never make any mistakes.
People may not see mistakes they don't understand.
Feeling confident always means you are doing well.
Teachers cannot find students' grammar mistakes.
q.why: 第 3 段：If you don't know much grammar, you can't see your own grammar mistakes——不懂的地方，連錯了都看不出來。

q.q: Leo just started learning chess. After winning two games against his little brother, he says he can beat anyone in his school. Based on the reading, what is the best advice for Leo?
opts: Stop playing chess because he is only a beginner.
Tell everyone at school that he is the best player.
Play stronger players and ask for their advice.
Keep playing only against his little brother.
q.why: 第 5 段：Everyone is a beginner at something…ask a teacher or a friend to check your work——找更強的人對弈並請教，才看得到自己的不足。

b.title: Unskilled and Unaware: Inside the Dunning-Kruger Studies
text: In 1995, a man in Pittsburgh robbed two banks in broad daylight without wearing a mask. When police arrested him, he was genuinely confused. He had rubbed lemon juice on his face, believing it would make him invisible to security cameras. The story caught the attention of David Dunning, a psychologist at Cornell University. If someone could be that wrong and that confident, Dunning wondered, how often do ordinary people misjudge their own abilities?

Together with his graduate student Justin Kruger, Dunning designed a series of experiments, published in 1999 under the memorable title "Unskilled and Unaware of It." Cornell students took tests of logical reasoning, English grammar and humor, and then estimated how their scores compared with those of their classmates.

The results were striking. Students who scored in the bottom quarter, on average around the 12th percentile, believed they had performed better than about 60 percent of their peers. Meanwhile, the top performers slightly underestimated themselves, apparently assuming that a task they found easy must be easy for everyone.

Dunning and Kruger argued that poor performers suffer a double burden. The knowledge required to give a correct answer is the same knowledge required to recognize a correct answer. Without it, people not only make mistakes but also fail to notice them. Encouragingly, when the researchers gave some low scorers a short lesson in logic, their self-assessments became more accurate.

The study has limits, however. Its participants were American university students, so the results may not apply equally to every culture or age group. Later researchers have also argued that part of the pattern could appear for purely statistical reasons, even if people judged themselves at random. The basic finding that we are often poor judges of our own skills is widely accepted, but its size is still debated.

Ironically, the effect is often misused. People cite it to mock others as foolish, yet the original point was that everyone is vulnerable in areas where they lack expertise. The real lesson is not "other people are clueless" but "check your own confidence."
tz: 1995 年，匹茲堡一名男子在光天化日之下、沒戴面罩就搶了兩家銀行。警方逮捕他時，他是真心感到困惑。他在臉上抹了檸檬汁，相信這樣監視器就拍不到他。這個故事引起了康乃爾大學心理學家大衛・達寧的注意。達寧想：如果有人能錯得這麼離譜又這麼有自信，那麼一般人錯估自己能力的情況有多常見？
達寧和他的研究生賈斯汀・克魯格設計了一系列實驗，1999 年以令人印象深刻的標題〈能力不足卻渾然不覺〉發表。康乃爾大學的學生做了邏輯推理、英文文法和幽默感的測驗，然後估計自己的分數和同學相比如何。
結果十分驚人。分數在最後四分之一的學生，平均約在第 12 百分等級，卻以為自己表現贏過大約六成的同儕。同時，表現最好的學生則略微低估自己，似乎認為自己覺得簡單的題目，對每個人一定也很簡單。
達寧和克魯格主張，表現差的人承受著雙重負擔：答對題目需要的知識，和辨認出正確答案需要的知識是同一套。缺少這些知識，人們不只會犯錯，也看不出自己犯了錯。令人振奮的是，研究人員讓部分低分者上了一堂簡短的邏輯課後，他們的自我評估變得比較準確。
不過，這項研究有它的限制。受試者是美國大學生，所以結果不一定同樣適用於每種文化或年齡層。後來的研究者也主張，即使人們隨機評估自己，這個模式也有一部分可能純粹因為統計原因而出現。「我們常常不太會評判自己的能力」這個基本發現被廣泛接受，但效應有多大仍有爭論。
諷刺的是，這個效應常被誤用。人們引用它來嘲笑別人愚蠢，但原本的重點是：每個人在自己缺乏專業的領域都可能犯這種錯。真正的教訓不是「別人什麼都不懂」，而是「檢查你自己的自信」。

ph.exzh: 小偷在光天化日之下偷走了腳踏車。

q.q: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
opts: How Lemon Juice Fooled Bank Security Cameras
Daily Life of a Cornell University Student
Why the Unskilled Often Overrate Themselves
Why Logic Tests Are Unfair to Most Students
q.why: 全文從搶匪故事（第 1 段）引入，說明實驗結果（第 3 段）、原因（第 4 段）與限制（第 5 段）——能力不足者常高估自己。

q.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
opts: The robber knew from the start that the lemon juice would not work.
A short logic lesson helped some weak students judge themselves.
The top students greatly overestimated their own test scores.
The study included people of many different ages and cultures.
q.why: 第 4 段：when the researchers gave some low scorers a short lesson in logic, their self-assessments became more accurate。第 1 段搶匪真心相信；第 3 段高分者略為低估；第 5 段受試者只有美國大學生。

q.q: What is the main purpose of paragraph 1?
opts: To explain how the police catch bank robbers
To describe the results of the 1999 study
To criticize the use of security cameras
To introduce the study with a real-life example
q.why: 第 1 段用檸檬汁搶匪的真實故事，引出達寧想研究的問題：一般人有多常錯估自己的能力。

q.q: In paragraph 3, the word “striking” is closest in meaning to ___.
opts: very noticeable
very violent
quite boring
hard to measure
q.why: 第 3 段：The results were striking——接著描述低分者大幅高估自己，結果非常引人注目。

q.q: What does the “double burden” in paragraph 4 suggest?
opts: Weak performers have to take twice as many tests as others.
Weak performers lack the very skill needed to judge their work.
Strong performers carry the heavy work for weaker classmates.
Weak performers notice their mistakes but are too shy to admit them.
q.why: 第 4 段：答對需要的知識＝辨認正確答案需要的知識；缺少它就 fail to notice them——缺乏判斷自己的能力。

q.q: A classmate laughs at a friend's mistake and says, “That's the Dunning-Kruger effect. He's just stupid.” Based on the passage, what is the best reply?
opts: The effect can apply to anyone, including us.
You're right; the effect proves he is foolish.
The effect only happens to bank robbers.
The effect was proven false in 1999.
q.why: 第 6 段：the original point was that everyone is vulnerable in areas where they lack expertise；真正的教訓是 check your own confidence。

tr.en: The knowledge required to give a correct answer is the same knowledge required to recognize a correct answer.
tr.zh: 答對題目需要的知識，和辨認出正確答案需要的知識是同一套。

tr.en: The story caught the attention of David Dunning, a psychologist at Cornell University.
tr.zh: 這個故事引起了康乃爾大學心理學家大衛・達寧的注意。

tr.en: The real lesson is not "other people are clueless" but "check your own confidence."
tr.zh: 真正的教訓不是「別人什麼都不懂」，而是「檢查你自己的自信」。

st.m: The basic finding that we are often poor judges of our own skills is widely accepted, but its size is still debated.
st.mz: 達寧和克魯格 1999 年的研究發現能力差的人常高估自己，因為缺乏判斷對錯的能力；這個發現大致被接受，但研究有限制，效應大小仍有爭議。
t: Together with his graduate student Justin Kruger, Dunning designed a series of experiments, published in 1999 under the memorable title "Unskilled and Unaware of It."
The results were striking.
Dunning and Kruger argued that poor performers suffer a double burden.
The study has limits, however.
st.c: The real lesson is not "other people are clueless" but "check your own confidence."

c.title: Is the Dunning-Kruger Effect Real?
text: Few findings in psychology have escaped the laboratory as successfully as the Dunning-Kruger effect. The phrase appears in political arguments, office jokes and countless online comment sections, usually accompanied by a graph showing confidence soaring at the start of learning, plunging into a "valley of despair," and slowly recovering as expertise grows. The graph is memorable. It is also not from the original research.

What David Dunning and Justin Kruger actually reported, in a 1999 paper that later earned them a satirical Ig Nobel Prize, was more modest. When Cornell students estimated their performance on tests of logic, grammar and humor, those in the bottom quarter overestimated their standing dramatically, while those at the top slightly underestimated theirs. The authors attributed the gap to a "double burden": incompetence deprives people of the very skills needed to recognize it.

Critics have since questioned whether this explanation is necessary. Their key argument is statistical. Two well-known tendencies, regression toward the mean and the widespread belief that one is above average, can produce a strikingly similar chart even when no one lacks insight. In 2016, a team led by the educational researcher Edward Nuhfer showed that random, meaningless numbers could generate a pattern resembling the famous result, which suggests that part of the original effect may be an artifact of the way the data were plotted.

Other researchers have tried to measure the effect more carefully. Using methods designed to avoid these statistical traps, the psychologists Gilles Gignac and Marcin Zajenkowski reported in 2020 that the evidence for the effect was considerably weaker than the classic graph implies.

Dunning has responded that the effect survives such corrections, pointing to studies in which people's errors were measured directly rather than inferred from averages. The debate, in other words, is less about whether people misjudge themselves than about how large the problem is and why it arises.

Ironically, the popularity of the concept may illustrate the very bias it describes. Many people who invoke the Dunning-Kruger effect have never read the study, yet speak about it with great confidence, often to dismiss others as ignorant. The research itself pointed in the opposite direction: everyone has areas in which they cannot see the limits of their own knowledge.

Perhaps the most defensible conclusion is a humble one. The relationship between skill and self-knowledge is real but messier than a viral graph suggests, and the best protection against overconfidence is not a label for other people but a habit of seeking feedback on oneself.
tz: 心理學裡很少有發現像達克效應這樣，成功地走出實驗室。這個詞出現在政治爭論、辦公室玩笑和數不清的網路留言區，通常還附上一張圖：信心在學習初期飆高，接著跌進「絕望之谷」，再隨著專業增長慢慢回升。這張圖令人難忘，但它也不是出自原始研究。
大衛・達寧和賈斯汀・克魯格在 1999 年那篇論文（後來還讓他們拿到帶有諷刺意味的搞笑諾貝爾獎）中真正報告的內容，其實比較保守。康乃爾學生估計自己在邏輯、文法和幽默測驗上的表現時，最後四分之一的人大幅高估了自己的排名，而頂尖的人則略為低估。作者把這個落差歸因於「雙重負擔」：能力不足，讓人正好缺少辨認出自己能力不足所需要的那些技能。
此後，批評者質疑這個解釋是否必要。他們的主要論點在統計上。兩種常見的傾向——向平均數迴歸，以及人們普遍相信自己高於平均——即使沒有人缺乏自知之明，也能畫出一張驚人相似的圖。2016 年，教育研究者愛德華・努弗帶領的團隊證明，隨機、毫無意義的數字也能產生類似那個著名結果的模式，這表示原始效應有一部分可能只是資料畫圖方式造成的假象。
其他研究者則嘗試更謹慎地測量這個效應。心理學家吉爾斯・吉納克和馬爾欽・札任考斯基使用專門避開這些統計陷阱的方法，在 2020 年報告：支持這個效應的證據比經典圖表所暗示的弱得多。
達寧回應說，這個效應在經過這類校正後依然存在，並舉出一些直接測量人們錯誤、而非從平均值推論的研究。換句話說，這場爭論的重點不在於人會不會錯估自己，而在於問題有多大、又為什麼會發生。
諷刺的是，這個概念的流行，可能正好示範了它所描述的偏誤。許多援引達克效應的人從沒讀過那項研究，卻說得信心十足，而且常用來貶低別人無知。研究本身指向的其實是相反的方向：每個人都有看不見自己知識極限的領域。
或許最站得住腳的結論是一個謙虛的結論。能力和自知之明之間的關係確實存在，但比一張爆紅的圖更複雜；而對抗過度自信最好的保護，不是給別人貼標籤，而是養成為自己尋求回饋的習慣。

ph.ex: The book is accompanied by a free CD.
ph.exzh: 這本書附贈一張免費 CD。

ph.zh: 把 A 歸因於 B
ph.ex: She attributed her success to hard work.
ph.exzh: 她把成功歸因於努力。

ph.zh: 剝奪 A 的 B；使 A 失去 B
ph.ex: The noise deprived us of sleep.
ph.exzh: 噪音讓我們睡不著。

ph.ex: Scientists point to rising sea levels as proof.
ph.exzh: 科學家舉出海平面上升作為證據。

ph.ex: He missed the bus. In other words, he'll be late.
ph.exzh: 他錯過公車了。換句話說，他會遲到。

ph.ex: Good writers seek feedback from readers.
ph.exzh: 好作家會向讀者尋求回饋。

q.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
opts: The effect has been fully proven, and the famous graph is accurate.
The effect was invented as a joke and has no scientific basis.
The effect is real but smaller and messier than its popular image.
Statistics cannot tell us anything useful about confidence.
q.why: 第 3–4 段提出統計批評，第 5 段指爭論在於「多大、為何」，第 7 段：real but messier than a viral graph suggests。

q.q: In paragraph 3, the word “artifact” is closest in meaning to ___.
opts: a false result caused by the method
an ancient object found underground
a skill that develops with practice
a reliable sign of low ability
q.why: 第 3 段：隨機數字也能畫出類似的圖，所以效應可能是 an artifact of the way the data were plotted——畫圖方式造成的假象。

q.q: What can be inferred about the “valley of despair” graph in paragraph 1?
opts: It was the main chart in the 1999 paper by Dunning and Kruger.
It was spread by others rather than drawn by Dunning and Kruger.
It was created by Nuhfer's team using random numbers.
It proves that confidence always rises as skill grows.
q.why: 第 1 段：The graph is memorable. It is also not from the original research——這張圖是後來流傳的，不是原研究畫的。

q.q: The author's attitude toward the Dunning-Kruger effect is best described as ___.
opts: openly hostile
blindly enthusiastic
completely indifferent
cautious and balanced
q.why: 作者同時呈現原研究（第 2 段）、批評（第 3–4 段）和回應（第 5 段），結論是 real but messier——謹慎而平衡。

q.q: What is the function of paragraph 6?
opts: To give new statistical evidence against the whole theory
To describe the details of the original experiment
To explain why the Ig Nobel Prize was awarded
To point out an irony in how the idea is popularly used
q.why: 第 6 段以 Ironically 開頭：引用者沒讀過研究卻很有自信，正好示範了這個偏誤。

q.q: An online commenter writes, “Science has proven that stupid people are always the most confident.” Based on the passage, which response is most reasonable?
opts: Agree, because the 1999 study proved it in all cultures.
Disagree, because the effect was shown to be completely fake.
Research suggests a weaker, more complex link than that.
Agree, since the famous graph comes straight from the study.
q.why: 第 4 段證據比經典圖弱；第 5 段效應仍存在但大小有爭議；第 7 段 real but messier——不是「完全成立」也不是「完全假的」。

st.m: The debate, in other words, is less about whether people misjudge themselves than about how large the problem is and why it arises.
st.mz: 達克效應的原始發現受到統計方法的質疑，爭論重點已不是人會不會高估自己，而是效應有多大、原因為何；流行的曲線圖也不是出自原研究，最好的做法是檢視自己而非嘲笑別人。

a.title: Twelve Seconds That Changed the World
text: On December 17, 1903, a strange machine made of wood and cloth rolled along a track on a windy beach in North Carolina, in the United States. Then it rose into the air. It flew for only 12 seconds and traveled about 37 meters, but it was the first powered airplane flight in history.

The pilot was Orville Wright. He and his older brother, Wilbur, did not go to college. They ran a small bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. Working with bicycles taught them a lot about balance, light machines and careful building.

The brothers worked on their idea for years. They studied birds and watched how they turned in the wind. They built gliders and a small wind tunnel to test different wing shapes. Many of their tests failed, but they kept trying and wrote down what they learned.
On that cold morning, they made four flights. The last one, with Wilbur as the pilot, lasted 59 seconds. Only five people were there to see it, and many newspapers did not believe the news at first.
Today, millions of people fly every day. But it all started with two brothers who were curious, patient and not afraid to fail.

b.title: How Two Bicycle Makers Solved the Problem of Flight
text: By the end of the 1800s, many inventors were trying to build a flying machine, and most of them were failing in public. Engines were becoming lighter and more powerful, so the main difficulty was no longer getting off the ground. It was staying in control once you were in the air. On December 17, 1903, two brothers from Ohio became the first to solve that problem with a powered aircraft.

Wilbur and Orville Wright had no university degrees and no government funding. They earned their money by building and repairing bicycles in Dayton. This background turned out to be an advantage. A bicycle is unstable on its own but can be balanced by a skilled rider, and the brothers believed an airplane should work the same way: the pilot, not the machine, should keep it steady.

To give the pilot that control, they developed a system called wing warping. By using cables to twist the ends of the wings slightly, the pilot could raise one side and lower the other, much as a bird adjusts its feathers. Combined with a movable rudder, this allowed the aircraft to turn and bank safely.

The brothers were also careful scientists. When their early gliders performed worse than expected, they suspected that the published data on wing design were wrong. In 1901 they built their own wind tunnel and tested about two hundred small wing shapes. The results allowed them to design far more efficient wings and propellers.

Their approach contrasted sharply with that of Samuel Langley, a respected scientist who received large public grants. Just nine days before the Wrights' success, Langley's machine plunged into the Potomac River at launch for the second time. Newspapers mocked the failure, and few reporters paid attention when two unknown bicycle makers flew near a remote beach.

Recognition came slowly. Only after public demonstrations in France and the United States in 1908 did the world accept what the brothers had achieved. Their story remains a reminder that careful testing can matter more than money or fame.
tz: 到了 1800 年代末，許多發明家都在嘗試打造飛行機器，而大多數人都在眾目睽睽下失敗。引擎變得越來越輕、越來越有力，所以主要的困難已經不是離開地面，而是升空之後如何保持控制。1903 年 12 月 17 日，兩位來自俄亥俄州的兄弟，成為第一個用動力飛機解決這個問題的人。
韋爾伯和奧維爾・萊特既沒有大學學位，也沒有政府資助。他們在代頓靠製造和修理腳踏車賺錢。這樣的背景後來反而成了優勢。腳踏車本身不穩，卻能被熟練的騎士保持平衡；兄弟倆相信飛機也該這樣運作：讓它保持穩定的是駕駛，而不是機器本身。
為了讓駕駛擁有這種控制力，他們發展出一套叫「機翼扭轉」的系統。駕駛用纜線把機翼末端稍微扭轉，就能讓一邊升高、另一邊降低，就像鳥調整羽毛一樣。再配合可以活動的方向舵，飛機就能安全地轉彎和傾斜。
兄弟倆也是細心的科學家。他們早期的滑翔機表現不如預期時，他們懷疑已發表的機翼設計資料有誤。1901 年，他們自己做了一個風洞，測試了大約兩百種小型機翼形狀。這些結果讓他們設計出效率高得多的機翼和螺旋槳。
他們的做法和薩謬爾・蘭利形成強烈對比；蘭利是一位受人尊敬、獲得大筆公共補助的科學家。就在萊特兄弟成功的九天前，蘭利的機器在發射時第二度栽進波多馬克河。報紙嘲笑這次失敗，而當兩個默默無名的腳踏車製造商在偏遠海灘附近飛上天時，幾乎沒有記者注意到。
世人的肯定來得很慢。直到 1908 年他們在法國和美國公開示範之後，全世界才承認兄弟倆的成就。他們的故事至今仍提醒我們：細心的測試可能比金錢或名氣更重要。

c.title: Who Really Invented the Airplane?
text: Ask an American who invented the airplane and the answer will almost certainly be the Wright brothers. Ask a Brazilian and you may hear a different name: Alberto Santos-Dumont. The disagreement is not merely patriotic. It reveals how much the answer depends on what we decide an "airplane" and a "flight" really are.

The case for the Wrights is strong. On December 17, 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright made a controlled, powered flight lasting 12 seconds, and his brother Wilbur later flew for 59 seconds. The brothers kept careful records, photographed the first flight and, crucially, solved the problem of steering an aircraft in three dimensions, which their rivals had largely ignored.

Critics, however, point to the conditions. The Flyer took off from a wooden rail into a strong headwind, and from 1904 the brothers used a weight-driven catapult to launch their aircraft. In Paris in 1906, by contrast, Santos-Dumont's 14-bis rose from the ground on its own wheels in front of a crowd and official observers. To his supporters, a true airplane must be able to take off unaided, and only he met that test.

A few historians have gone further, arguing that a German-American mechanic named Gustave Whitehead flew in Connecticut in 1901. Most experts reject the claim, noting that it rests on later recollections and a newspaper report without a surviving photograph. The controversy shows how heavily priority disputes depend on evidence, and how easily that evidence can be lost.

The Wrights' own behavior added fuel to the debate. Determined to profit from their invention, they spent years in court defending their patent against other builders, most famously Glenn Curtiss. Some historians argue that these lawsuits slowed American aviation; by the First World War, the United States lagged well behind Europe in aircraft design.

Even the Smithsonian Institution became involved. For decades it suggested that Langley's failed machine had been capable of flight first, prompting Orville to send the original Flyer to a museum in London. Only after the Smithsonian publicly corrected its position in 1942 did the aircraft return to the United States, where it arrived in 1948.

Perhaps the most reasonable conclusion is that invention is rarely a single moment. Asking who was first may matter less than asking what each person contributed. The Wrights deserve credit for the decisive breakthrough in control, while others contributed in ways that history has been slower to recognize.
tz: 問美國人是誰發明了飛機，答案幾乎一定是萊特兄弟；問巴西人，你可能會聽到另一個名字：阿爾貝托・桑托斯－杜蒙。這個分歧不只是愛國情緒，它揭示了答案在多大程度上取決於我們如何定義「飛機」和「飛行」。
支持萊特兄弟的理由很充分。1903 年 12 月 17 日，在北卡羅來納州小鷹鎮附近，奧維爾・萊特完成了一次持續 12 秒、可控制的動力飛行，他的哥哥韋爾伯之後又飛了 59 秒。兄弟倆留下詳細紀錄、拍下了第一次飛行的照片，而且關鍵的是，他們解決了在三度空間中操控飛機的問題，而這是對手們大多忽略的。
然而，批評者指出了當時的條件。飛行者號是從木製軌道、迎著強勁逆風起飛的，而且從 1904 年起，兄弟倆用重錘驅動的彈射器來發射飛機。相較之下，1906 年在巴黎，桑托斯－杜蒙的 14-bis 號在群眾和官方觀察員面前，靠自己的輪子離地升空。對他的支持者而言，真正的飛機必須能在無外力協助下起飛，而只有他通過了這項考驗。
還有少數歷史學家更進一步，主張一位名叫古斯塔夫・懷特海德的德裔美國技師在 1901 年就於康乃狄克州飛行過。大多數專家不接受這個說法，指出它依據的是事後的回憶和一篇沒有留下照片的報導。這場爭議顯示，「誰是第一」的爭論有多麼依賴證據，而證據又多麼容易遺失。
萊特兄弟自己的作為也讓爭論火上加油。為了從發明中獲利，他們多年來在法庭上捍衛自己的專利，對抗其他飛機製造者，其中最有名的是葛倫・柯蒂斯。有些歷史學家認為，這些官司拖慢了美國航空的發展；到第一次世界大戰時，美國在飛機設計上已遠遠落後歐洲。
連史密森尼學會也捲入其中。數十年來，它暗示蘭利那架失敗的機器才是最先具備飛行能力的，這促使奧維爾把原始的飛行者號送到倫敦的一家博物館。直到史密森尼在 1942 年公開更正立場後，這架飛機才回到美國，並於 1948 年抵達。
或許最合理的結論是：發明很少只是一個瞬間。問「誰是第一」，可能不如問「每個人貢獻了什麼」來得重要。萊特兄弟在操控上的決定性突破值得肯定，而其他人的貢獻，歷史則比較晚才認可。

a.title: The First Voice from Space
text: On December 18, 1958, the United States sent a satellite into space. It was called SCORE. A few days later, people around the world heard something amazing on the radio: a voice from space. It was the voice of President Dwight Eisenhower.

Of course, the president was not in space. Before the launch, he recorded a short Christmas message on tape. The satellite carried the tape around the Earth and sent the message back down by radio. In it, he wished people everywhere peace on Earth.

SCORE was not very big or powerful. Its batteries lasted only about two weeks, and it fell back to Earth a month later. But it showed that a satellite could help people send messages across long distances.

Today, thousands of satellites go around our planet. They help us watch TV, check the weather, find our way with maps on our phones and even use the Internet in faraway places. When you watch a soccer game from another country, a satellite may be helping you.
So the next time you look up at the night sky, remember that it is busy. Many of the tiny moving lights you see are not stars. They are satellites, carrying our voices and pictures around the world.
tz: 1958 年 12 月 18 日，美國把一顆衛星送上太空，它叫做 SCORE。幾天後，世界各地的人從收音機裡聽到一件很神奇的事：一個來自太空的聲音。那是艾森豪總統的聲音。
當然，總統並不在太空。發射之前，他用錄音帶錄了一段簡短的聖誕節談話。衛星帶著錄音帶繞著地球轉，再用無線電把訊息傳回地面。在這段談話裡，他祝福世界各地的人享有地上的和平。
SCORE 不是很大，功能也不強。它的電池只撐了大約兩個星期，一個月後就掉回地球了。但它證明了衛星可以幫助人們把訊息傳到很遠的地方。
現在，有數千顆衛星繞著我們的星球運行。它們幫助我們看電視、查天氣、用手機地圖找路，甚至在偏遠的地方上網。當你看另一個國家的足球比賽時，可能就有一顆衛星在幫你。
所以下次你抬頭看夜空時，記得天上其實很忙碌。你看到的許多會移動的小光點並不是星星，而是衛星，正把我們的聲音和畫面送到世界各地。

b.title: From SCORE to Today: How Satellites Carry Our Messages
text: In December 1958, just over a year after the Soviet Union shocked the world with Sputnik, the United States launched a satellite called SCORE. Its mission was kept so secret that even many of the engineers who worked on the rocket did not know about it. A few days before Christmas, radio listeners heard a recorded message from President Dwight Eisenhower explaining that his voice was coming to them from a satellite circling in outer space.

SCORE was simple. It could receive a message from the ground, store it on a tape recorder and send it back down later. Its batteries died after about two weeks, but it proved a crucial idea: a machine in orbit could act as a relay station, passing signals between distant points on Earth.

The idea had been described years earlier by the science-fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke. In 1945, he suggested that a satellite about 36,000 kilometers above the equator would circle the planet exactly once a day. Seen from the ground, it would seem to hang still in the sky, so a dish could point at it permanently. Three such satellites, Clarke noted, could cover almost the entire world.

His prediction came true in the 1960s. In 1962, a satellite called Telstar carried the first live television pictures across the Atlantic, and in 1964, a satellite in Clarke's special orbit helped broadcast the Tokyo Olympics to viewers in the United States.

These high satellites have one weakness, however. Because signals must travel so far, there is a short but noticeable delay, which can make phone calls awkward. That is one reason companies today are launching thousands of smaller satellites into much lower orbits, where signals arrive faster and the Internet can reach ships, villages and disaster zones.

In a little more than half a century, satellites have gone from a secret experiment to an invisible part of daily life. Every time you check a map or watch a match from overseas, you are relying on the idea that SCORE first tested.
tz: 1958 年 12 月，就在蘇聯以史普尼克號震驚世界一年多之後，美國發射了一顆叫 SCORE 的衛星。它的任務保密到連許多參與火箭工作的工程師都不知道。聖誕節前幾天，收音機聽眾聽到艾森豪總統預錄的談話，說明他的聲音正從一顆在外太空繞行的衛星傳給他們。
SCORE 很簡單。它能接收地面傳來的訊息，存在錄音機裡，之後再傳回地面。它的電池大約兩週後就耗盡了，但它證明了一個關鍵的構想：在軌道上的機器可以充當中繼站，在地球上相距遙遠的兩地之間傳遞訊號。
這個構想其實在多年前就被科幻作家亞瑟・克拉克描述過。1945 年，他提出：一顆位於赤道上空約 36,000 公里的衛星，會剛好一天繞地球一圈。從地面看，它就像靜止掛在天空中，所以碟型天線可以一直對準它。克拉克指出，只要三顆這樣的衛星，就能涵蓋幾乎整個世界。
他的預言在 1960 年代成真。1962 年，一顆叫電星（Telstar）的衛星首次把電視直播畫面傳過大西洋；1964 年，一顆位於克拉克所說特殊軌道上的衛星，協助把東京奧運轉播給美國觀眾。
不過，這些高軌道衛星有一個缺點。因為訊號必須傳得非常遠，會有短暫但明顯的延遲，讓講電話變得不太順暢。這也是為什麼現在有公司把數千顆較小的衛星送進低得多的軌道：在那裡訊號傳得更快，網路也能到達船隻、村莊和災區。
在短短半個多世紀裡，衛星從一項祕密實驗，變成日常生活中看不見的一部分。每當你查地圖或看海外的比賽時，你依靠的正是 SCORE 最早測試的那個構想。

c.title: A Crowded Sky: The Hidden Costs of Connecting Everyone
text: When SCORE broadcast a Christmas message from orbit in December 1958, it was one of only a handful of human-made objects circling the Earth. Today the picture is radically different. Thousands of active satellites now orbit the planet, many of them belonging to a few private "mega-constellations" designed to beam the Internet to every corner of the globe. The benefits are real, but so are the costs, and the debate over who should pay them has only begun.

The case for these networks is compelling. Roughly a third of the world's population still lacks reliable Internet access, much of it in rural or mountainous regions where laying cables is too expensive. Low-orbit satellites can bring connections to remote schools, ships at sea and communities struck by disasters. In recent conflicts, they have also kept people online when ground networks were destroyed.

Astronomers, however, have raised alarms. Satellites reflect sunlight, leaving bright streaks across telescope images, and their radio signals can interfere with observations of faint objects in deep space. Some companies have responded by darkening their satellites, but researchers argue that such measures reduce rather than remove the problem. For many people, the night sky itself is a shared heritage that no company should be allowed to fill.

A more urgent danger is debris. In 1978, the NASA scientist Donald Kessler warned that if enough objects crowded low orbit, collisions could create fragments that cause further collisions, producing a chain reaction. In the worst case, certain orbits could become too dangerous to use for generations. With more satellites launched each year, the scenario now named after him is no longer purely theoretical.

Supporters of the new networks reply that modern satellites are designed to fall out of orbit and burn up within a few years once they stop working, unlike older spacecraft that remain in space for decades. They also point out that a handful of governments have created far more debris through anti-satellite weapons tests than any private company has.

The deeper problem is governance. Space law was largely written in the 1960s, when only governments could reach orbit, and it says little about how much of a shared resource a single company may occupy. Without clearer international rules, decisions affecting everyone are being made by a small number of firms.

None of this means satellites should be abandoned; few technologies have done more to connect humanity. It does suggest that the sky above us is not unlimited, and that deciding how to use it should not be left to whoever launches first.
tz: 1958 年 12 月 SCORE 從軌道上播出聖誕談話時，它是當時少數幾個繞地球運行的人造物體之一。今天的景象截然不同。現在有數千顆運作中的衛星繞著地球，其中許多屬於少數幾個民營的「巨型衛星星系」，目的是把網路傳送到全球每個角落。好處是真的，代價也是真的，而由誰來承擔代價的爭論才剛開始。
支持這些網路的理由很有說服力。全世界大約三分之一的人口仍然沒有可靠的網路，其中許多住在鄉村或山區，在那裡鋪設纜線太昂貴。低軌衛星能把網路帶到偏遠的學校、海上的船隻和受災的社區。在近年的衝突中，當地面網路被摧毀時，它們也讓人們保持連線。
然而，天文學家已經提出警告。衛星會反射陽光，在望遠鏡影像上留下明亮的光痕，它們的無線電訊號也可能干擾對深太空暗弱天體的觀測。有些公司的回應是把衛星塗暗，但研究人員認為這類措施只能減輕、無法消除問題。對許多人來說，夜空本身就是共同的遺產，不該允許任何公司把它填滿。
更迫切的危險是太空碎片。1978 年，NASA 科學家唐納德・凱斯勒警告：如果低軌道擠滿了夠多物體，碰撞會產生碎片，碎片又引發更多碰撞，形成連鎖反應。最糟的情況下，某些軌道可能好幾個世代都危險到無法使用。隨著每年發射的衛星越來越多，這個以他命名的情境已不再只是理論。
新網路的支持者回應說，現代衛星在停止運作後的幾年內就會脫離軌道、燒毀，不像舊式太空船會在太空中停留數十年。他們也指出，少數幾個國家政府透過反衛星武器試驗所製造的碎片，遠比任何民營公司都多。
更深層的問題在於治理。太空法大多寫於 1960 年代，當時只有政府能進入軌道，它幾乎沒有規範單一公司可以占用多少共同資源。在缺乏更明確國際規則的情況下，影響每個人的決定正由少數幾家公司做出。
這一切並不代表我們應該放棄衛星；很少有科技比它更能連結人類。但這確實表示，我們頭頂的天空不是無限的，而如何使用它，不該交給最先發射的人來決定。

topic: A Christmas Carol: The Book That Shaped a Holiday
zh: 《小氣財神》：一本形塑節日的書
src: Charles Dickens Museum, London · British Library · Children's Employment Commission report (1843)

a.title: Scrooge and the Three Ghosts
text: On December 19, 1843, a short book went on sale in London. It was called A Christmas Carol, and it was written by Charles Dickens. By Christmas Eve, all 6,000 copies were sold. Today, more than 180 years later, people around the world still know its story.

The story is about Ebenezer Scrooge, a rich old man who loves money and hates Christmas. When people wish him a merry Christmas, he says, "Bah! Humbug!" He pays his worker, Bob Cratchit, very little, even though Bob's young son, Tiny Tim, is sick.

One Christmas Eve, three ghosts visit Scrooge. The first shows him his past, when he was young and kind. The second shows him how other people are spending Christmas, including Bob's poor but happy family. The third shows him a sad future, where no one cares that he has died.
Scrooge wakes up the next morning a new man. He buys a big turkey for the Cratchits, gives money to the poor and becomes like a second father to Tiny Tim.

Dickens knew about being poor. When he was 12, his father was sent to prison for not paying his debts, and young Charles had to work in a factory. He wanted his book to remind readers to be kind to people in need.

故事的主角是艾比尼澤・史古基，一個愛錢又討厭聖誕節的有錢老人。別人祝他聖誕快樂時，他會說：「呸！胡說八道！」他付給員工鮑伯・克拉奇的薪水很少，即使鮑伯的小兒子小提姆生病了也一樣。
某個聖誕夜，三個鬼魂來拜訪史古基。第一個讓他看見自己的過去，那時他年輕又善良。第二個讓他看見別人怎麼過聖誕節，包括鮑伯那貧窮卻快樂的一家。第三個讓他看見一個悲傷的未來：他死了，卻沒有人在乎。
第二天早上，史古基醒來後彷彿變了一個人。他為克拉奇一家買了一隻大火雞，捐錢給窮人，還像第二個父親一樣照顧小提姆。
狄更斯很了解貧窮是什麼滋味。他 12 歲時，父親因為還不出債而被關進監獄，小查爾斯只好到工廠工作。他希望這本書能提醒讀者善待需要幫助的人。

b.title: How A Christmas Carol Changed the Holiday
text: Few books have shaped a holiday as much as A Christmas Carol. Published by Charles Dickens on December 19, 1843, the short novel sold out its first printing of 6,000 copies by Christmas Eve. Its main character, the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge, became so famous that his name entered the dictionary as a word for a person who hates spending money.

Dickens wrote the book in about six weeks, but its roots went much deeper. Earlier that year, he had read a government report describing children working long hours in mines and factories, and he had visited a school for children from the poorest parts of London. He first planned to write a political pamphlet about the problem. Then he decided that a story would reach far more hearts.

The plot is simple. On Christmas Eve, Scrooge is visited by the ghost of his former business partner, Jacob Marley, and then by three spirits who show him his past, his present and a possible future. Seeing the poor but loving family of his clerk, Bob Cratchit, and learning that their sick son, Tiny Tim, may die, Scrooge finally changes his ways.

The book's influence on how Christmas is celebrated has been enormous. It helped popularize the idea of Christmas as a time for family gatherings, generous giving and kindness to strangers. Phrases like "Merry Christmas" became more common, and Scrooge's cry of "Bah! Humbug!" is still quoted today.

Ironically, the book was not a great financial success for its author. Dickens insisted on an expensive design with colored pictures but kept the price low, so his profits were disappointing. He later earned far more by reading the story aloud to large audiences, which he did for the rest of his life.
Since then, the tale has been adapted into countless plays, films and cartoons. Its lasting appeal may lie in its central promise: that it is never too late for a person to change.
tz: 很少有書像《小氣財神》這樣深深形塑了一個節日。查爾斯・狄更斯在 1843 年 12 月 19 日出版這部短篇小說，首刷 6,000 本在聖誕夜前就賣光了。書中主角、吝嗇的艾比尼澤・史古基出名到他的名字被收進字典，用來指討厭花錢的人。
狄更斯大約六週就寫完這本書，但它的根源要深得多。那年稍早，他讀了一份政府報告，裡面描述兒童在礦坑和工廠長時間工作；他也參觀了一所專收倫敦最貧窮地區孩子的學校。他原本打算寫一本談這個問題的政治小冊子，後來決定，一個故事能打動更多人的心。
情節很簡單。聖誕夜，史古基先是被已故生意夥伴雅各・馬里的鬼魂拜訪，接著又有三個幽靈讓他看見他的過去、現在和一個可能的未來。看到職員鮑伯・克拉奇貧窮卻充滿愛的家庭，又得知他們生病的兒子小提姆可能會死，史古基終於改過自新。
這本書對人們過聖誕節方式的影響非常巨大。它幫助推廣了「聖誕節是家人團聚、慷慨付出、善待陌生人的時節」這個觀念。「聖誕快樂」之類的說法變得更普遍，而史古基那句「呸！胡說八道！」至今仍常被引用。
諷刺的是，這本書對作者來說在財務上並不算成功。狄更斯堅持用有彩色插圖的昂貴設計，卻把售價壓低，所以利潤令人失望。他後來靠著對大批聽眾朗讀這個故事賺了多得多的錢，而且這件事他做了一輩子。
從那時起，這個故事被改編成無數的舞台劇、電影和卡通。它歷久不衰的魅力，或許就在於它核心的承諾：一個人要改變，永遠不嫌晚。

c.title: Can a Story Change Society?
text: In the spring of 1843, Charles Dickens read a government report on child labor and was horrified. Children, some barely old enough for school, were working long hours in mines and factories. His first impulse was to write a pamphlet, a direct appeal for reform. Within months he had changed his mind, promising that a different kind of response would land with far greater force. That response was A Christmas Carol, published on December 19 of the same year.

Dickens's bet was that fiction could achieve what statistics could not. A report might inform readers, but a story could make them feel. By placing a sick child, Tiny Tim, at the center of a family that cannot afford proper food or medicine, Dickens turned an abstract social problem into a face that readers could not easily forget.

In one sense, the bet paid off spectacularly. The book sold out within days, and its picture of Christmas as a season of generosity spread across the English-speaking world. Some writers even describe Dickens as the man who "invented" the modern Christmas, although that claim is exaggerated: Christmas trees, cards and carols were already gaining popularity in Victorian Britain, and the first commercial Christmas card appeared in the very same year.

Critics, however, have long questioned the book's solution. Poverty in the Carol is relieved not by better laws or higher wages but by the sudden kindness of one wealthy man. Scrooge raises Bob Cratchit's salary and sends a turkey, yet the system that kept thousands of families like the Cratchits poor remains untouched. Read this way, the story may comfort comfortable readers more than it challenges them.

Defenders reply that this criticism misreads the book. Dickens was not writing a policy paper; he was trying to change attitudes, which must shift before laws do. The most chilling scene, in which the Ghost of Christmas Present reveals two starving children named Ignorance and Want, is aimed squarely at society, not at Scrooge alone. Moreover, Dickens supported education and reform throughout his life.

The debate is not merely historical. Modern charity campaigns still rely on single, personal stories rather than numbers, because research suggests people respond more generously to one identifiable victim than to statistics about millions. The risk Dickens faced remains: emotion can move people to give without moving them to ask why help is needed.
Perhaps the fairest judgment is that stories and policies do different work. A Christmas Carol could not fix child labor, but it helped create readers who cared whether someone did.
tz: 1843 年春天，查爾斯・狄更斯讀了一份關於童工的政府報告，大為震驚。有些孩子才剛到上學的年紀，就在礦坑和工廠裡長時間工作。他的第一個衝動是寫一本小冊子，直接呼籲改革。但幾個月內他就改變了主意，承諾要用另一種方式回應，而且力道會大得多。那個回應就是同年 12 月 19 日出版的《小氣財神》。
狄更斯賭的是：小說能做到統計數字做不到的事。一份報告也許能讓讀者知道，但一個故事能讓他們感受。他把生病的小提姆放在一個買不起像樣食物和藥品的家庭中心，把抽象的社會問題變成一張讀者難以忘懷的臉。
從某個角度來看，這場賭注獲得了驚人的回報。這本書幾天內就賣光，它所描繪「聖誕節是慷慨的季節」的景象傳遍了英語世界。有些作家甚至把狄更斯形容為「發明」現代聖誕節的人，不過這種說法太誇張了：聖誕樹、聖誕卡和聖誕頌歌在維多利亞時代的英國早已越來越流行，而第一張商業聖誕卡也正好在同一年問世。
然而，批評者長久以來質疑這本書提出的解方。《小氣財神》裡的貧窮，不是靠更好的法律或更高的工資緩解，而是靠一個有錢人突如其來的善心。史古基給鮑伯・克拉奇加薪、送去一隻火雞，但讓成千上萬像克拉奇這樣的家庭陷於貧窮的制度卻絲毫未變。這樣讀來，這個故事帶給生活舒適的讀者的，可能是安慰多於挑戰。
辯護者則回應，這種批評誤讀了這本書。狄更斯寫的不是政策報告；他想改變的是態度，而態度必須先轉變，法律才會跟著改變。書中最令人不寒而慄的一幕——現在之靈揭示兩個名叫「無知」與「匱乏」的飢餓孩子——矛頭直指整個社會，而不只是史古基一人。此外，狄更斯一生都支持教育與改革。
這場爭論不只是歷史問題。現代的慈善募款仍然仰賴單一、個人化的故事，而不是數字，因為研究顯示，比起數百萬人的統計數據，人們對一個可辨認的受害者會更慷慨。狄更斯當年面對的風險依然存在：情感能讓人們捐款，卻未必能讓他們追問為什麼需要幫助。
或許最公允的評價是：故事和政策做的是不同的工作。《小氣財神》無法解決童工問題，但它幫助培養出一群在乎是否有人去解決的讀者。

a.title: Four Light Bulbs in the Desert
text: On December 20, 1951, scientists in the desert of Idaho, in the United States, watched four light bulbs. Suddenly, the bulbs began to glow. This may not sound exciting, but it was a big moment in history. It was the first time that electricity from nuclear energy was used to light anything.

The electricity came from a machine called EBR-I. Inside it, tiny pieces of a metal called uranium split apart. This made a lot of heat. The heat was used to make steam, and the steam turned a machine that made electricity. The next day, EBR-I made enough electricity to power its whole building.
Today, nuclear power plants make about one-tenth of the world's electricity. They do not make smoke like coal plants, so they don't add much carbon dioxide to the air.

But nuclear power has problems too. Accidents, like the one in Fukushima, Japan, in 2011, can be very dangerous. Nuclear waste also stays harmful for thousands of years, so it must be stored very carefully.

Taiwan shut down its last nuclear reactor in 2025, but people still argue about whether to use nuclear energy again. What do you think? The four little light bulbs in Idaho started a big question that we are still trying to answer.

這些電來自一台叫 EBR-I 的機器。在它裡面，一種叫做鈾的金屬的微小粒子分裂開來，產生大量的熱。這些熱被用來製造蒸汽，蒸汽再推動一台發電的機器。第二天，EBR-I 發的電已經足夠供應整棟建築使用。
現在，核能電廠大約產生全世界十分之一的電。它們不像燃煤電廠那樣冒煙，所以不太會增加空氣中的二氧化碳。
但核能也有問題。像 2011 年日本福島那樣的事故可能非常危險。核廢料也會有害好幾千年，所以必須非常小心地存放。
台灣在 2025 年關閉了最後一座核子反應爐，但大家仍在爭論要不要再使用核能。你怎麼想呢？愛達荷州那四顆小燈泡，開啟了一個我們至今還在努力回答的大問題。

b.title: Nuclear Power: How It Works and Why It Divides Us
text: On December 20, 1951, at a remote research station in the Idaho desert, a team of scientists led by Walter Zinn switched on four ordinary light bulbs. The bulbs were powered by an experimental reactor called EBR-I, and they marked the first time nuclear energy had produced usable electricity. The team chalked their names on a wall to celebrate the occasion, and the signatures can still be seen today.

The basic principle is surprisingly similar to that of a coal-fired plant. In both, heat boils water, the resulting steam spins a turbine, and the turbine drives a generator. The difference lies in the source of the heat. In a nuclear reactor, the nuclei of heavy atoms such as uranium are split apart, a process called fission, releasing enormous amounts of energy from a very small amount of fuel.

EBR-I was also designed to test a bold idea. As a "breeder" reactor, it aimed to produce more nuclear fuel than it consumed, and by 1953 it had shown that this was possible. Yet the reactor's history also included a warning: in 1955, during an experiment, part of its core melted. No one was hurt, but the incident showed how quickly things could go wrong.

Today, nuclear plants supply roughly a tenth of the world's electricity. Supporters point out that they release very little carbon dioxide while running and, unlike solar or wind power, can generate electricity day and night regardless of the weather.

Opponents raise serious concerns. Major accidents such as Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011 forced well over a hundred thousand people from their homes. Used fuel remains dangerously radioactive for thousands of years, and few countries have built a permanent place to store it. New plants are also expensive and often take more than a decade to build.

Taiwan shut down its last nuclear reactor in 2025, yet the debate there, as elsewhere, continues. Seventy-five years after four bulbs flickered on in Idaho, the question is less about whether nuclear power works than about whether its benefits are worth its risks.
tz: 1951 年 12 月 20 日，在愛達荷州沙漠中一座偏遠的研究站，由華特・齊恩帶領的科學家團隊打開了四顆普通的燈泡。這些燈泡的電來自一座叫 EBR-I 的實驗反應爐，標誌著核能第一次產生可用的電力。團隊成員用粉筆在牆上寫下自己的名字來慶祝，這些簽名至今仍看得到。
它的基本原理和燃煤電廠出奇地相似：兩者都是用熱把水煮沸，產生的蒸汽推動渦輪機，渦輪機再帶動發電機。差別在於熱的來源。在核子反應爐裡，像鈾這樣的重原子的原子核被分裂開來，這個過程叫核分裂，能從極少量的燃料釋放出巨大的能量。
EBR-I 也是為了測試一個大膽的構想而設計的。作為一座「滋生」反應爐，它的目標是產生比消耗的還多的核燃料，而到了 1953 年，它證明了這是可行的。然而，這座反應爐的歷史也包含一個警訊：1955 年在一次實驗中，它的爐心有一部分熔毀了。沒有人受傷，但這起事件顯示事情可能多快就出錯。
現在，核能電廠供應全世界大約十分之一的電力。支持者指出，核電廠運轉時幾乎不排放二氧化碳，而且不像太陽能或風力，無論天氣如何都能日夜發電。
反對者則提出嚴重的疑慮。1986 年的車諾比和 2011 年的福島等重大事故，各自迫使超過十萬人離開家園。用過的燃料在數千年內仍具危險的放射性，而很少國家建好了永久存放的地方。新電廠也很昂貴，而且常常要花十多年才能蓋好。
台灣在 2025 年關閉了最後一座核子反應爐，但那裡和其他地方一樣，爭論仍在持續。在四顆燈泡於愛達荷州亮起七十五年後，問題已經不太在於核能行不行得通，而在於它的好處是否值得它的風險。

c.title: Is Nuclear Power the Answer to Climate Change?
text: When four light bulbs flickered to life in the Idaho desert on December 20, 1951, powered by a reactor called EBR-I, many people believed nuclear energy would soon make electricity almost free. That promise was never fulfilled. Yet seventy-five years later, nuclear power is once again at the center of a fierce debate, this time not because of its cheapness but because of the climate crisis.

The argument in its favor begins with carbon. Measured over their entire life cycle, nuclear plants emit about as little greenhouse gas per unit of electricity as wind farms, and far less than coal or gas. Unlike wind and solar, they produce power around the clock, which makes them attractive to countries trying to cut emissions without risking blackouts. Several governments that once planned to abandon nuclear energy have recently reconsidered.

Safety, supporters argue, is often misjudged. Disasters such as Chernobyl and Fukushima were terrifying, but measured by deaths per unit of energy produced, nuclear power has caused far fewer than fossil fuels, whose air pollution quietly kills millions of people every year. Fear, in this view, has been shaped more by vivid images than by statistics.

Critics respond that statistics do not capture everything. A single serious accident can make a region uninhabitable for decades and destroy public trust overnight. Spent fuel remains hazardous for thousands of years, and although Finland is building the world's first permanent deep repository, most countries still keep their waste in temporary sites. Asking future generations to guard our garbage, they say, is a moral problem as well as a technical one.

There is also the matter of cost and time. Recent projects in Europe and the United States have run years behind schedule and billions over budget. Meanwhile, the price of solar panels and batteries has fallen dramatically. If the goal is to cut emissions quickly, critics argue, money spent on slow, expensive reactors might achieve more if invested in renewables.

For Taiwan, the debate is especially sharp. The island shut down its last reactor in 2025, relies heavily on imported fuel, sits in an earthquake zone and has limited land for solar and wind farms. Each of these facts strengthens one side of the argument or the other, which helps explain why the issue remains so divisive.

Perhaps the most honest conclusion is that there is no risk-free option. Every energy source involves trade-offs, and the real question is which risks a society is willing to accept, and who gets to decide.
tz: 1951 年 12 月 20 日，四顆燈泡在愛達荷州沙漠中由一座叫 EBR-I 的反應爐點亮時，許多人相信核能很快就會讓電幾乎免費。這個承諾從未實現。然而七十五年後，核能再度成為激烈爭論的焦點，這一次不是因為它便宜，而是因為氣候危機。
支持核能的論點從碳開始。若以整個生命週期來計算，核電廠每度電排放的溫室氣體和風力發電場差不多少，而且遠低於燃煤或燃氣。不像風力和太陽能，核電能全天候供電，這讓它對想減碳又不想冒停電風險的國家很有吸引力。好幾個曾經打算放棄核能的政府，最近都重新考慮了。
支持者認為，人們常常誤判核能的安全性。車諾比和福島等災難令人驚恐，但若以每單位發電量造成的死亡人數來衡量，核能造成的死亡遠少於化石燃料，而化石燃料造成的空氣污染每年默默奪走數百萬人的生命。從這個觀點來看，恐懼更多是由鮮明的畫面而非統計數字塑造的。
批評者回應，統計數字無法涵蓋一切。一次嚴重的事故就可能讓一個地區數十年無法居住，並在一夜之間摧毀大眾的信任。用過的核燃料在數千年內都具有危險性，雖然芬蘭正在興建全世界第一座永久的深層處置場，大多數國家仍把核廢料放在臨時的地點。他們說，要求未來世代替我們看守垃圾，既是技術問題，也是道德問題。
還有成本和時間的問題。歐洲和美國近年的核電計畫延宕多年、超出預算數十億。同時，太陽能板和電池的價格大幅下降。批評者認為，如果目標是快速減碳，把錢花在又慢又貴的反應爐上，或許不如投資再生能源來得有效。
對台灣來說，這場爭論特別尖銳。台灣在 2025 年關閉了最後一座反應爐，高度依賴進口燃料，位處地震帶，能用來設置太陽能和風力發電場的土地也有限。這些事實各自強化了爭論中的某一方，這也說明了為什麼這個議題至今仍如此分歧。
或許最誠實的結論是：沒有零風險的選項。每一種能源都有取捨，真正的問題是一個社會願意承擔哪些風險，以及由誰來決定。

a.title: Far from Home, Close to Us
text: Every year on December 18, the United Nations celebrates International Migrants Day. A migrant is a person who moves to another country to live or work. Today, about 280 million people around the world live outside the country where they were born.

Many migrants live in Taiwan, too. More than 700,000 migrant workers from countries such as Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand work here. Some build our roads and make things in factories. Others work on fishing boats far out at sea. Many take care of older people in their homes.

Life is not always easy for them. They are far away from their families, and some can only go home once every few years. They have to learn a new language and new customs. Some work very long hours, and some must pay a lot of money to the companies that found them their jobs.

Migrants also bring a lot to Taiwan. You can taste their food at night markets and hear their languages on trains. Many children in Taiwan have a parent who came from another country, and schools now teach Southeast Asian languages.
What can you do? Start with something small: smile and say hello. Learn how to say "thank you" in Indonesian or Vietnamese. A little kindness can help someone far from home feel welcome.

台灣也有很多移民。超過七十萬名來自印尼、越南、菲律賓和泰國等國家的移工在這裡工作。有些人幫我們蓋馬路、在工廠製造東西；有些人在遠洋的漁船上工作；還有很多人在家裡照顧長輩。
他們的生活並不總是很輕鬆。他們離家人很遠，有些人好幾年才能回家一次。他們必須學習新的語言和新的習俗。有些人工作時間很長，有些人還得付一大筆錢給幫他們找到工作的公司。
移工也為台灣帶來很多東西。你可以在夜市吃到他們的食物，在火車上聽到他們的語言。台灣有很多孩子的爸爸或媽媽來自其他國家，現在學校也有教東南亞語言。
你可以做什麼呢？從小事開始：微笑、打聲招呼。學會用印尼語或越南語說「謝謝」。一點點善意，就能讓離家很遠的人感到受歡迎。

b.title: Why the World Marks International Migrants Day
text: On December 18, 1990, the United Nations adopted an international agreement to protect the rights of migrant workers and their families. Ten years later, it chose that date as International Migrants Day. The day is meant to remind the world that the roughly 280 million people living outside their country of birth are not just numbers in a report, but workers, parents, students and neighbors.

People migrate for many reasons. Some are pushed out by war, disaster or poverty; others are pulled by better jobs, education or family. Most move legally and by choice, and many send part of their wages home. These payments, known as remittances, add up to hundreds of billions of US dollars a year and help pay for food, school fees and medical care in their home countries.

Taiwan is a clear example of how much a society can depend on migrants. More than 700,000 migrant workers, mostly from Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand, work in its factories, on its construction sites and fishing boats, and in homes caring for elderly and disabled people. As Taiwan's population ages, families increasingly rely on these caregivers.

Their contribution, however, has not always been matched by protection. Many workers pay heavy fees to recruitment agencies before they arrive, leaving them in debt. Home caregivers are not covered by Taiwan's main labor law, so their working hours can be extremely long. Workers on distant-water fishing boats have reported abuse at sea, far from any inspector.

Change is happening, though slowly. Labor groups and migrants themselves have pushed for reforms, and schools now teach the languages of Southeast Asian immigrant families. Many young Taiwanese grow up with a parent born abroad, which makes the question of belonging a personal one.
International Migrants Day asks a simple question: if migrants help build our cities and care for our grandparents, what do we owe them in return? Fair treatment may be the least we can offer.
tz: 1990 年 12 月 18 日，聯合國通過了一項保護移工及其家人權利的國際公約。十年後，聯合國選定這一天為國際移民日。這個日子是要提醒世人：全球大約 2 億 8 千萬住在出生國以外的人，不只是報告裡的數字，而是工作者、父母、學生和鄰居。
人們遷移的原因很多。有些人是被戰爭、災難或貧窮逼離家鄉；有些人則是被更好的工作、教育或家人吸引。大多數人是合法且自願遷移的，而且很多人會把部分工資寄回家。這些被稱為「僑匯」的款項，每年加起來高達數千億美元，幫忙支付他們母國家人的食物、學費和醫療費用。
台灣清楚說明了一個社會可以多麼依賴移民。超過七十萬名移工，大多來自印尼、越南、菲律賓和泰國，在台灣的工廠、工地、漁船上工作，也在家庭裡照顧長者和身心障礙者。隨著台灣人口老化，家庭越來越依賴這些看護。
然而，他們的貢獻並不總是換來相應的保障。許多移工在來台之前就得付給仲介高額費用，因此背負債務。家庭看護不受台灣主要勞動法律的保障，所以工時可能非常長。遠洋漁船上的漁工也曾通報在海上遭到虐待，那裡離任何檢查人員都很遠。
改變正在發生，只是很緩慢。勞工團體和移工自己都在爭取改革，學校現在也教授東南亞新住民家庭的語言。許多台灣年輕人的父母有一方在國外出生，這讓「歸屬」成為切身的問題。
國際移民日提出一個簡單的問題：如果移工幫我們建設城市、照顧我們的祖父母，那我們該回報他們什麼？公平對待，或許是我們最起碼能給的。

c.title: Guests, Workers or Neighbors?
text: In the 1960s, Switzerland recruited large numbers of foreign workers on the assumption that they would work for a few years and then leave. Many stayed, raised families and became part of Swiss society, prompting the writer Max Frisch to make a famous observation: "We asked for workers, and human beings came." Six decades later, his remark still captures the central tension in how wealthy societies think about migration.

That tension is especially visible in East Asia. Taiwan, Japan and South Korea all have rapidly aging populations and some of the lowest birth rates in the world. Factories, farms, fishing fleets and families caring for elderly relatives increasingly depend on workers from Southeast Asia. Yet for decades, policy in the region treated these workers as temporary guests: useful for their labor, but not expected to settle.

Supporters of a more open approach argue that this model is both unfair and unsustainable. It is unfair because people who contribute years of work and taxes are denied the security and rights that would let them plan a future. It is unsustainable because, as populations shrink, countries will increasingly compete for the same workers, and those that offer dignity and a path to belonging will attract them.

Skeptics raise legitimate questions. Some worry that large-scale migration could hold down wages for low-paid local workers or strain housing and public services. Others fear that rapid change may weaken social trust. Most economic research finds that the overall effect of migration on local wages is small, but averages can hide real pressures on particular communities, and dismissing these concerns tends to fuel resentment rather than reduce it.

Policies in the region have begun to shift. In 2022, Taiwan introduced a scheme allowing experienced migrant workers to qualify for longer stays and, eventually, a route toward permanent residency, while Japan has created new visas for skilled foreign workers. Critics note that these reforms remain limited and that problems such as debt to recruitment agencies persist.

Ultimately, the debate is about more than economics. It concerns whether a society sees migrants as a resource to be managed or as people who may become fellow citizens. Frisch's sentence is a reminder that the second view is not a choice a country can avoid forever: workers who stay long enough will become neighbors, whether or not the law recognizes it.
International Migrants Day, observed each December 18, offers an occasion to ask which kind of society we wish to be.
tz: 1960 年代，瑞士以「外籍勞工工作幾年就會離開」為前提，招募了大批外籍勞工。許多人留了下來、成家，成為瑞士社會的一部分，這促使作家馬克斯・弗里施說出一句名言：「我們要的是勞工，來的卻是人。」六十年後，這句話仍點出了富裕社會思考移民問題時的核心矛盾。
這種矛盾在東亞特別明顯。台灣、日本和南韓的人口都快速老化，出生率也是全世界最低的之一。工廠、農場、漁船隊，以及照顧年長親人的家庭，都越來越依賴來自東南亞的勞工。然而數十年來，這個地區的政策都把這些勞工當作暫時的客人：需要他們的勞力，卻不期待他們定居。
主張更開放做法的人認為，這種模式既不公平也無法持續。說它不公平，是因為貢獻了多年勞力和稅金的人，卻得不到能讓他們規劃未來的保障和權利。說它無法持續，是因為隨著人口減少，各國會越來越常爭搶同一批勞工，而那些能提供尊嚴和歸屬途徑的國家，才會吸引到他們。
懷疑者提出了合理的問題。有些人擔心大規模移民可能壓低本地低薪勞工的工資，或讓住房和公共服務負擔過重。也有人擔心快速的變化可能削弱社會信任。大多數經濟研究發現，移民對本地工資的整體影響很小，但平均值可能掩蓋特定社區承受的真實壓力，而輕忽這些疑慮往往只會助長不滿，而不是減少不滿。
這個地區的政策已經開始轉變。2022 年，台灣推出一項方案，讓有經驗的移工能取得較長的居留資格，最終還有一條通往永久居留的途徑；日本也為具技能的外籍勞工設立了新的簽證。批評者指出，這些改革仍然有限，而仲介債務等問題依然存在。
說到底，這場爭論不只關乎經濟。它關乎一個社會把移民看成需要管理的資源，還是可能成為同胞的人。弗里施的話提醒我們，第二種看法不是一個國家能永遠迴避的選擇：待得夠久的勞工終將成為鄰居，無論法律承不承認。
每年 12 月 18 日的國際移民日，提供了一個機會，讓我們問問自己想成為什麼樣的社會。

a.title: An Email Before the Flight
text: Hi Yu-ting, great news! My plans for the exchange trip are ready. I will fly from London to Taipei next month, and I can't wait to meet you and your family.

Here is my flight information. Airline: Sky Bird Airlines, Flight SB 108. Date: Monday, January 4. Leaves London Heathrow at 9:40 p.m. Arrives at Taoyuan Airport at 7:40 p.m. on Tuesday, Taiwan time. The flight is about 14 hours long, so I will sleep on the plane.

My mom says I should get to the airport three hours early. First, I will check in and drop off my big suitcase. Then I will go through security. I can't bring big bottles of water, so I will buy a drink after security.

Did you know that December 7 is International Civil Aviation Day? My teacher told us about it. Every day, thousands of planes fly safely around the world because countries work together and follow the same rules.
Can you or your dad pick me up at the airport? If my flight is late, I will send you a message. Also, what should I bring? Is it cold in Taipei in January?
See you soon! Emma

b.title: The Rules That Keep the Sky Safe
text: Every day, tens of thousands of passenger planes take off, cross borders and land in countries where the pilots may not speak the local language. That this happens so smoothly is no accident. It depends on an agreement signed more than eighty years ago.

On December 7, 1944, while World War II was still being fought, representatives of dozens of countries meeting in Chicago signed the Convention on International Civil Aviation, usually called the Chicago Convention. They knew that after the war, air travel could either bring nations closer together or become a new source of conflict, so they wanted shared rules from the very start.

The convention led to the creation of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which became a United Nations agency in 1947. Today, ICAO sets standards that member countries agree to follow: how runways are marked, how air traffic controllers talk to pilots and how accidents are investigated. English became the common language of international aviation, which is why a pilot from Brazil and a controller in Japan can understand each other.

To mark the 50th anniversary of the agreement, ICAO created International Civil Aviation Day in 1994, and the UN officially recognized it two years later. The day reminds people that safe flights are the result of cooperation, not luck. Airports and airlines often mark it with exhibitions, open days and talks for students.

Aviation also faces difficult questions. Planes produce a small but growing share of the greenhouse gases that warm the planet, and the industry is under pressure to cut its emissions through cleaner fuels and more efficient aircraft. Some people argue that we should simply fly less; others believe new technology will solve the problem.
Either way, the lesson of 1944 still matters. When countries agree on common rules, millions of strangers can travel together safely every day.
tz: 每天都有數以萬計的客機起飛、跨越國界，降落在機師可能不會說當地語言的國家。這一切能如此順利，並不是偶然，而是靠著八十多年前簽下的一份協定。
1944 年 12 月 7 日，第二次世界大戰還在進行，數十個國家的代表在芝加哥開會，簽署了《國際民用航空公約》，通常稱為《芝加哥公約》。他們知道戰後的空中交通可能讓各國更親近，也可能成為新的衝突來源，所以希望從一開始就有共同的規則。
這份公約促成了國際民航組織（ICAO）的成立，它在 1947 年成為聯合國的專門機構。如今 ICAO 制定會員國同意遵守的標準：跑道怎麼標示、航管人員怎麼和機師對話、事故怎麼調查。英語成為國際航空的共同語言，所以巴西的機師和日本的航管人員能聽懂彼此。
為了紀念這份協定五十週年，ICAO 在 1994 年訂立國際民航日，兩年後聯合國正式承認。這一天提醒人們：飛行安全是合作的成果，而不是運氣。機場和航空公司常在這天舉辦展覽、開放參觀日和給學生的講座。
航空業也面臨難題。飛機排放的溫室氣體占全球暖化氣體的比例雖小，卻在增加，業界正承受壓力，要用更乾淨的燃料和更有效率的飛機減少排放。有些人主張我們乾脆少搭飛機；另一些人則相信新科技能解決問題。
無論如何，1944 年的教訓仍然重要：當各國同意共同的規則，數百萬互不相識的人每天才能一起安全地旅行。

c.title: Rules of the Air: Cooperation at 30,000 Feet
text: When the Chicago Convention was signed on December 7, 1944, its authors faced a puzzle that still shapes air travel. Each state, the treaty declared, has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory. Yet aviation only works if aircraft can cross that airspace freely. The history of international flying is, in many ways, the story of how nations have balanced control with cooperation.

The compromise was practical. Rather than settling every commercial question at once, countries agreed on separate deals covering the so-called freedoms of the air: the right to fly over a country, to land for fuel, to carry passengers between two nations, and so on. Many of these rights are still negotiated pair by pair, which is why some routes are crowded with competing airlines while others are served by a single carrier.

Where the convention truly succeeded was in technical standards. Its annexes, regularly updated by the International Civil Aviation Organization, cover everything from pilot licensing to airport design. Because these standards are shared, an aircraft certified in one country can be maintained and flown almost anywhere. Combined with better technology and accident investigations that focus on learning rather than blame, this cooperation has helped make commercial flying one of the safest ways to travel.

Cooperation, however, has limits. Membership in ICAO is tied to the United Nations system, and Taiwan, which is not a member, has long argued that it should be able to take part in the organization's meetings because the Taipei Flight Information Region handles a large volume of international traffic. It attended the ICAO Assembly as a guest in 2013 but has not been invited since. Supporters say aviation safety should not depend on politics; the organization's decisions, however, are made by its member states.

The newest test is climate change. In 2016, ICAO members agreed on a scheme called CORSIA, under which airlines offset growth in their carbon emissions by paying for projects that reduce emissions elsewhere. Critics argue that offsets are hard to verify and allow the industry to delay real cuts; supporters reply that a global agreement is better than a patchwork of national rules.

More than eighty years after Chicago, the central question has not changed: how can countries that guard their own skies work together closely enough to keep everyone in the air safe, and the planet livable?
tz: 1944 年 12 月 7 日簽署《芝加哥公約》時，起草者面對一個至今仍影響航空旅行的難題。公約宣告：每個國家對其領土上空擁有完全且排他的主權。然而，航空要運作，飛機就必須能自由穿越這些空域。國際航空的歷史，在許多方面，就是各國如何在主權控制與合作之間取得平衡的故事。
當時的妥協很務實。各國沒有一次解決所有商業問題，而是另外簽訂涵蓋所謂「航權」的協議：飛越一國領空的權利、降落加油的權利、在兩國之間載客的權利等等。許多航權至今仍是兩國兩國地談判，這就是為什麼有些航線擠滿互相競爭的航空公司，有些卻只有一家在飛。
公約真正成功的地方在技術標準。由國際民航組織定期更新的附約，涵蓋從機師執照到機場設計的一切。因為這些標準是共通的，在一國取得認證的飛機幾乎可以在任何地方維修和飛行。再加上更好的科技，以及著重學習而非究責的事故調查，這種合作讓商業飛行成為最安全的交通方式之一。
然而，合作也有極限。ICAO 的會籍與聯合國體系綁在一起，而不是會員的台灣長期主張應該能參與該組織的會議，因為台北飛航情報區處理大量國際航班。台灣在 2013 年以貴賓身分出席 ICAO 大會，此後就再也沒有受邀。支持者說航空安全不應取決於政治；然而，這個組織的決定是由會員國做出的。
最新的考驗是氣候變遷。2016 年，ICAO 會員國同意一項名為 CORSIA 的機制：航空公司出錢資助其他地方的減碳計畫，來抵銷自己碳排放的成長。批評者認為抵銷很難查證，還讓業界得以拖延真正的減排；支持者則回應，一個全球協議總比各國規則東拼西湊來得好。
芝加哥會議八十多年後，核心問題依然沒變：守護自己天空的各國，要如何密切合作，才能讓空中的每個人安全，也讓地球適合居住？

topic: The Geminids: December's Shooting Stars
zh: 雙子座流星雨：十二月的流星
src: NASA · American Meteor Society · Taipei Astronomical Museum

a.title: Look Up! Shooting Stars in December
text: Do you like looking at the night sky? Next week, you may be able to see a lot of shooting stars. Every December, the Geminid meteor shower lights up the sky.
Shooting stars are not really stars. They are small pieces of rock and dust from space. When they hit the air around Earth very fast, they get very hot and burn. We see them as bright lines of light.

Most meteor showers come from comets, which are big balls of ice and dust. The Geminids are different. They come from a strange rock called 3200 Phaethon. Scientists think it is an asteroid, but it leaves dust behind like a comet.

The Geminids are one of the best meteor showers of the year. This year, the best nights are December 13 and 14. On a dark night far from city lights, people may see dozens of shooting stars in one hour.

Here are some tips. Go to a dark place, like a beach or a mountain. Wear a warm jacket. Lie down and look up for at least 20 minutes. Your eyes need time to get used to the dark, so don't look at your phone!
You don't need a telescope. All you need is your eyes, a little patience and a clear sky. And don't forget to make a wish!
tz: 你喜歡看夜空嗎？下週你也許能看到很多流星。每年十二月，雙子座流星雨都會點亮夜空。
流星其實不是星星，而是來自太空的小石頭和塵埃。它們以極快的速度撞進地球周圍的空氣時，會變得非常熱而燃燒起來，我們就看到一道道明亮的光線。
大部分的流星雨來自彗星，彗星是由冰和塵埃組成的大球。雙子座流星雨不一樣，它來自一顆奇怪的岩石，叫做「3200 法厄同」。科學家認為它是一顆小行星，但它卻像彗星一樣留下塵埃。
雙子座流星雨是一年中最棒的流星雨之一。今年最佳的觀賞夜晚是 12 月 13 日和 14 日。在遠離城市燈光的黑暗夜晚，一小時內可能看到幾十顆流星。
這裡有一些小建議：到黑暗的地方，像是海邊或山上；穿上保暖的外套；躺下來往上看至少 20 分鐘。你的眼睛需要時間適應黑暗，所以不要看手機！
你不需要望遠鏡，只需要你的眼睛、一點耐心和晴朗的天空。還有，別忘了許個願！

b.title: The Geminids: A Meteor Shower With a Mystery
text: Every December, sky-watchers around the world look forward to the Geminid meteor shower, which many astronomers consider the strongest and most reliable shower of the year. In 2026, it is expected to peak on the nights of December 13 and 14.

A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by an object in space. As tiny particles, many no bigger than a grain of sand, rush into the atmosphere at tens of kilometers per second, friction with the air heats them until they glow. Because the particles travel along parallel paths, the meteors seem to come from a single point in the sky. For the Geminids, that point lies in the constellation Gemini, which gives the shower its name.

What makes the Geminids unusual is their source. Most showers are produced by comets, icy bodies that shed dust as they approach the Sun. The Geminids, however, are linked to 3200 Phaethon, an object discovered in 1983 that looks more like a rocky asteroid. Scientists are still debating how a rock can leave behind so much debris. One idea is that Phaethon passes so close to the Sun that its surface cracks in the heat, releasing dust.

Viewing conditions matter as much as the shower itself. Under a perfectly dark sky, an observer might count over a hundred meteors an hour, but light pollution in cities can reduce that to just a handful. This year, the moon will be only a thin crescent around the peak, so it should not spoil the show.

For students in Taiwan, the best plan is to leave the city, give your eyes about 20 minutes to adjust to the darkness and look at a wide area of sky rather than at one spot. Meteors are often easier to see after midnight. No equipment is needed, only patience, warm clothes and a clear night.
tz: 每年十二月，世界各地的觀星者都期待著雙子座流星雨，許多天文學家認為它是一年中最強、最穩定的流星雨。2026 年預計在 12 月 13 日和 14 日晚上達到極大期。
當地球穿過太空中某個天體留下的碎屑流時，就會出現流星雨。這些微小的顆粒很多不比一粒沙大，以每秒數十公里的速度衝進大氣層，與空氣摩擦而發熱，直到發光。因為這些顆粒沿著平行的路徑前進，流星看起來就像從天空中的同一個點射出。雙子座流星雨的這個點位在雙子座，流星雨也因此得名。
雙子座流星雨特別的地方在於它的來源。大多數流星雨由彗星產生——彗星是冰質天體，接近太陽時會散出塵埃。然而，雙子座流星雨和「3200 法厄同」有關，這個 1983 年發現的天體看起來更像一顆岩質小行星。科學家仍在爭論一顆岩石怎麼能留下這麼多碎屑。其中一個說法是，法厄同離太陽非常近，表面在高溫下裂開，釋放出塵埃。
觀賞條件和流星雨本身一樣重要。在完全黑暗的天空下，觀測者一小時可能數到一百多顆流星，但城市的光害可能讓數量降到只剩寥寥幾顆。今年極大期前後月亮只是細細的眉月，應該不會干擾觀賞。
對台灣的學生來說，最好的計畫是離開城市，給眼睛大約 20 分鐘適應黑暗，並且看一大片天空，而不是盯著同一個點。午夜之後流星通常比較容易看到。不需要任何器材，只要耐心、保暖的衣服和晴朗的夜晚。
